dek: Your flight got wrecked by the FAA ground stop, here's how to get your refund fast.

slides.label: The Stop
slides.text: Friday, Nov. 13, just after 4 p.m.: the FAA stopped *all departures nationwide* after a communications failure.

slides.label: The Damage
slides.text: More than *6,000 flights* were canceled Saturday, FlightAware says, including 21% at JFK and LaGuardia.

slides.label: What Caused It
slides.text: A contractor was switching old copper wire to fiber. The system *overloaded*. Officials say it wasn't a cyberattack.

slides.label: Your Refund
slides.text: If the airline canceled and you skipped the rebooking, you're owed a *full refund*, even on non-refundable tickets.

slides.label: The 3-Hour Rule
slides.text: A *significant delay* counts too: 3+ hours domestic, 6+ hours international delays.

slides.label: The Catch
slides.text: Accepted the rebooked flight or a voucher? You likely *gave up* your cash refund already.

slides.label: Free Changes
slides.text: *JetBlue* is waiving change fees for Nov. 13 to 15 flights, rebook through Wednesday, Nov. 18.

slides.label: 11 Days Out
slides.text: Thanksgiving is *11 days away*. Know your rights, keep your receipts, don't let a bad weekend cost you twice.

The FAA ground stop refund rules just became very real: if your flight out of JFK, LaGuardia or Newark got canceled during Friday's nationwide stop, you're owed your money back, automatic, no fighting required.

Here's what went down: a contractor switching old copper wire to fiber overloaded the system, grounding every departure in the country for more than four hours. By Saturday, over 6,000 flights were canceled, and NYC airports took the hit hardest.

The part people miss: if you took the rebooked flight or a voucher, you likely gave up your cash refund. But if you said no and skipped it, that refund hits your card within 7 business days, no exceptions, even on non-refundable fares.

caption_linkedin:
The FAA's nationwide ground stop on Friday was a four hour outage with a ripple effect that lasted the whole weekend. A contractor's fiber upgrade overloaded the air traffic control system, and by Saturday more than 6,000 flights were canceled, JFK and LaGuardia each lost 21% of their schedule.

For founders and operators, the lesson isn't about airlines, it's about what happens when infrastructure fails during peak load, and who eats the cost when it does. Here, federal rules already answered that question: if the airline canceled your flight, your refund is automatic, back to your original payment method, no negotiation required, even on non-refundable fares.

The catch is just as instructive: accept the workaround, the rebooked flight, the voucher, and you waive your claim to the original terms. Know what you are owed before you accept any substitute, in travel or in business.

Thanksgiving is 11 days out and another stress test is coming. Which matters more to you right now, speed of recovery or clarity of rights?
